notes.summary: Permitted bounded-product foundations are audited; radial normalization, bounded Stokes, and product pullbacks are derived. No BMP-dependent unbounded theorem is used.
notes.detailedSummary: The only non-elementary foundation used is the explicitly permitted bounded Bedford–Taylor/corrected-product theory of BGL §2.1. Its normalization differs by the positive factor 4π. This note derives the shell formula d(a^k), closed-background bounded mass invariance, and bounded product/pullback identities. The conditional nonclosed product is handled by an explicit finite truncation limit.
notes.text:
This is a mathematical foundation/application audit. The task permits local psh representatives and decreasing limits, normalized Fubini–Study geometry, elementary radial calculus, and BGL §2.1 bounded corrected products and locality. No A–G result is imported.

The public primary source checked is Boucksom, Guedj and Lu, “Volumes of Bott–Chern Classes”, DOI 10.1007/s42543-025-00105-2, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42543-025-00105-2. Its bounded-product section contains formulas (2.1)–(2.6) and Proposition 2.1; the publisher HTML displays the heading as 3.1. The permitted foundations supply symmetric multilinear bounded products, decreasing continuity, smooth-background expansion, plurifine locality, and positivity for positive currents. That source uses dd^c=2i∂bar∂, whereas the task uses 1/(4π) times this operator. Positive rescaling preserves the properties used. The adjoining global unbounded-product theorem requires BMP and is not invoked.

For bounded quasi-psh b_i and smooth θ_i, expand ∧(θ_i+dd^c b_i) into smooth factors and bounded dd^c-products. Locally write b_i=p_i−γ_i with bounded psh p_i and smooth γ_i. Smooth local regularization of p_i, followed by decreasing continuity, gives this expansion and its agreement with smooth wedges wherever the potentials are smooth. Pullback by a product projection commutes with these bounded products: regularize on the source chart, prove the identity for smooth functions, and pass to the decreasing limit on the product chart. Terms exceeding their factor's dimension vanish. These applications require neither closed backgrounds nor BMP.

Here is the needed bounded Stokes consequence. If h is closed positive and b is bounded h-psh on a compact m-fold, put T=h+dd^c b. Locally choose h=dd^c γ. The recursive bounded-product definition for the bounded psh function b+γ gives dd^c(bS)=(T−h)∧S for a closed bounded-product current S built from T and h. Subtracting the smooth γ contribution verifies the identity. Therefore globally
T^m−h^m=dd^c[b∑_{j=0}^{m−1}T^j∧h^{m−1−j}].
Pairing with 1 on the compact manifold gives ∫T^m=∫h^m. This is a bounded assertion, not unbounded mass invariance.

For the exact radial normalization, let r=∑|z_j|² and κ=dd^c b, b=log(1+r). If f(r) is smooth and a=rf', its complex Hessian has eigenvalues a/r with multiplicity k−1 and a'=f'+rf'' in the radial direction. For k≥2 it is semipositive exactly when a≥0 and a'≥0. With the task's dd^c, (dd^c f)^k has Euclidean density k!π^(−k)(f')^(k−1)(f'+rf''). Polar Euclidean volume has radial density π^k r^(k−1)/(k−1)!, so the radial mass is k a^(k−1)a' dr=d(a^k).

Writing x=r/(1+r), rb'=x. Consequently κ^k has radial density d(x^k)=k r^(k−1)/(1+r)^(k+1)dr, of total integral one. For f=b+U, the density of (κ+dd^c U)^k relative to κ^k is a^(k−1)a'/(x^(k−1)x'). This proves the normalization and shell formula used below.

A canonical extension fact is also elementary. Suppose f is psh on a punctured ball, f'≥0, and f→−∞ at its center. For ε_j decreasing to zero, cap f by the constant f(ε_j), extending the cap constantly inside r≤ε_j. Near the gluing sphere this is a maximum of psh functions, and near the center it is constant. The caps are psh and decrease to f with value −∞ at the center. Subtracting a smooth local background gives the genuine quasi-psh representative, including its pole.

Source evidence is retained in bgl_bounded_section.txt. The available web tool retrieved the public source; direct Python HTTPS retrieval was denied with Operation not permitted. No credentials, root article, private calculation, target-author argument, campaign, or report supplied a proof dependency. No supervised compute service is exposed; none was needed for these elementary proofs and light audits. Further artifacts and rerun commands are listed in n8.

notes.summary: A is proved: genuine nonlogarithmic κ-psh poles, mass one, smooth positive off-pole density, L1-only density, distinct ordinary types, and trivial multiplier ideals.
notes.detailedSummary: The flux aα=x+αT^(α−1)/(1+r) is strictly increasing from zero to one. The density behaves as α^k(1−α)r^(−k)L^(−k(1−α)−1), giving L1 but no Lp for p>1. Exponential integrability proves every finite-t ideal is trivial. The potential itself belongs to every finite Lp; the L1/no-Lp assertion concerns the density. No model or envelope identity is claimed.
notes.text:
Claim A is proved, interpreting its L1/no-Lp sentence as concerning qα. Put x=r/(1+r), T=1−log x, L=1−log r for small r, b=log(1+r), and
uα=1−T^α, fα=b+uα, aα=rfα'=x+αT^(α−1)/(1+r).
Direct differentiation gives
aα'=[1−αT^(α−1)+α(1−α)T^(α−2)/r]/(1+r)².
Since T≥1 and 0<α<1, both aα and aα' are strictly positive for r>0. The radial Hessian test in n1 makes fα psh on the punctured chart. Since fα→−∞, the decreasing caps in n1 give its canonical psh extension. The estimate |uα|≤C(1+|log r|^α) gives local integrability, indeed integrability of every finite power. Thus uα is genuinely κ-psh with value −∞ at o.

The homogeneous function x=∑_{j≥1}|z_j|²/∑_{j≥0}|z_j|² is globally smooth. Outside o, x>0; hence uα is smooth, including the hyperplane x=1 where it equals zero. Semipositivity extends there by smoothness.

The flux endpoints are aα(0)=0 and aα(∞)=1. The shell formula gives
qα=aα^(k−1)aα'/(x^(k−1)x')=(1+r)^(k+1)aα^(k−1)aα'/r^(k−1)>0.
Near x=1 this becomes aα^(k−1)(daα/dx)/x^(k−1), which is smooth and has value 1−α. Thus the density is smooth positive on the entire complement of o.

To identify the extended measure directly, use bounded κ-psh truncations uα,j=max(uα,−j). Bounded locality identifies their measures restricted to {uα>−j} with the smooth measure there. These restrictions increase to its extension by zero at o. Its mass is aα(∞)^k−aα(0)^k=1. The center is pluripolar, locally exhibited by log r, and receives no mass. No unbounded-product theorem is needed.

As r→0, T/L→1 and
 aα~αL^(α−1),
 aα'~α(1−α)r^(−1)L^(α−2),
 qα~α^k(1−α)r^(−k)L^(−β−1), β=k(1−α)>0.
The local L1 integral is comparable to ∫r^(−1)L^(−β−1)dr and converges. For p>1, the integral of qα^p is comparable to ∫r^(−k(p−1)−1)L^(−p(β+1))dr and diverges: substituting s=−log r produces exponentially growing exp(k(p−1)s) times a negative power of s. Away from the pole the density is smooth. Thus qα is L1 and belongs to no Lp, p>1. Uniform comparability gives the same conclusion relative to any smooth positive volume. In contrast, uα itself belongs to every finite Lp; an interpretation assigning the no-Lp assertion to the potential would be false.

If α<α̃, then uα̃≤uα and uα−uα̃=T^α̃−T^α→∞. Hence the ordinary types are distinct and strictly ordered. For each real t>0, exp(−tuα)=exp(t(T^α−1)) is integrable near o: eventually tT^α≤(k/2)L, whereas smooth radial volume decays as exp(−kL)dL. Every holomorphic germ is bounded on a smaller neighborhood, so its squared modulus times this weight is integrable. Therefore I(tuα)=O for every real t>0, with exactly the stated convention and no additional factor 2. No ordinary-model, ideal-model, or zero-obstacle identity is asserted.

The derivative formula is also checked symbolically in verify_radial.py. Rerun: python verify_radial.py > verification_output.txt. Execution is an algebraic audit, not the proof.

notes.summary: B–C are proved for nonnegative radial probability densities: actual compact solution, prescribed ordinary type and stretching class, radial uniqueness, and quantitative endpoint residual regularity without density-error derivative bounds.
notes.detailedSummary: The solution is obtained from Fq(r)=∫_0^r q d(x^k), Aq=Fq^(1/k), and U=−∫_r^∞(Aq−x)dt/t. The density tail yields Fq−aα^k=O(r^δL^(−k(1−α)−1)), giving all three residual estimates. Positive cumulative mass gives smoothness off the pole even at density zeros; the probability tail gives smoothness at infinity. The residual is Hölder with exponent min(1,2δ), C1 with zero gradient for δ≥1/2, and C2 with zero Hessian for δ≥1, including equality. U retains its canonical pole.
notes.text:
Assume B exactly: q≥0 is radial, smooth on P^k away from o including the entire hyperplane, has integral one, and g=q/qα−1 satisfies |g(r)|≤A r^δ near zero. No density-error derivative bound is assumed. Put S=aα^k and
Fq(r)=∫_0^r q(t)d(x(t)^k), H=Fq−S=∫_0^r g(t)dS(t), Aq=Fq^(1/k).
The tail hypothesis makes q positive near zero. Consequently Fq(r)>0 at every finite r>0, even where q itself vanishes. Also Fq≤1 and Fq(∞)=1. Thus Aq is smooth for r>0, nonnegative and nondecreasing.

Let β=k(1−α). From n2, S'≤C r^(−1)L^(−β−1) and S≥cL^(−β) for small r. Since L(t)^γ≤L(r)^γ for t≤r and γ<0,
|H|≤CA∫_0^r t^(δ−1)L(t)^(−β−1)dt≤(CA/δ)r^δL^(−β−1).
Hence H/S=O(r^δ/L). Restricting the neighborhood makes |H/S|≤1/2. Smoothness of the kth root on [1/2,3/2] gives
Δ=Aq−aα=aα[(1+H/S)^(1/k)−1]=O(r^δL^(α−2)). (1)
Differentiating the cumulative equation once uses only the density:
Aq'=(1+g)aα^(k−1)aα'/Aq^(k−1).
Therefore
Δ'=aα'[(1+g)(aα/Aq)^(k−1)−1]=O(r^(δ−1)L^(α−2)). (2)
No derivative of g occurs.

For normalization and smoothness at infinity, set η=1/(1+r). Smooth radial q has a smooth profile Q(η) at η=0. Indeed, on the transverse complex line in the chart z1=1, r=|τ|^(−2). The smooth rotationally invariant function q(1/|τ|²) has the form Q̃(|τ|²) with Q̃ smooth at zero. To see this by calculus, restrict to real τ and obtain a smooth even f. The identity f'(t)=t∫_0^1 f''(st)ds has a smooth even integral. Induction on differentiability then shows f(√y) is smooth for y≥0. Changing y to η proves the assertion. The same radial profile applies at every hyperplane point, and η is smooth there.

Probability normalization gives
1−Fq=J(η), J(η)=k∫_0^η Q(v)(1−v)^(k−1)dv.
This is smooth with J(0)=0; Aq=(1−J)^(1/k) is smooth near zero and equals one there. Since Aq−x=O(η), define
U(r)=−∫_r^∞[Aq(t)−x(t)]dt/t. (3)
The upper endpoint converges. Its derivative is U'=(Aq−x)/r, and its hyperplane value is zero. Moreover
dU/dη=−[Aq−(1−η)]/[η(1−η)]
is smooth at η=0 because the numerator vanishes there. Thus U is smooth across the full hyperplane, including its density zeros. At every finite r>0, Fq>0 gives smoothness. The local potential b+U has flux Aq, hence is psh by n1. Smooth extension at infinity preserves semipositivity. Its smooth off-pole measure is qκ^k by the shell formula.

The potential uα also satisfies (3), with aα in place of Aq. For the actual residual R=U−uα, initially defined only off o, R'=Δ/r. Bound (1) is integrable at zero, so R has a finite limit R0 and
R(r)−R0=∫_0^r Δ(t)dt/t.
Bounds (1)–(2) now give a finite C, on a small punctured neighborhood,
|R−R0|≤Cr^δL^(α−2),
|R'|≤Cr^(δ−1)L^(α−2),
|R''|=|Δ'/r−Δ/r²|≤Cr^(δ−2)L^(α−2). (4)
All primes are derivatives with respect to r. Constants can depend on α,k,δ,A and the neighborhood; the finite limit also depends on global data. These are precisely C's estimates.

Since U=uα+bounded residual near zero, U→−∞ and is locally integrable. The canonical psh caps in n1 give its value −∞ at o. It has no other pole. Truncations max(U,−j), bounded locality, and the integrability of q identify its extended measure with qκ^k extended by zero at o. Its mass is exactly one. This proves actual compact existence.

The residual extension is continuous on all P^k, hence bounded. Choose M≥0 with R≥−M. Then U≃uα in ordinary order, including the common pole. For each t≥1 take the genuine κ-psh potential a_t=uα−tM. For t>1,
t^(−1)a_t+(1−t^(−1))uα=uα−M≤U.
At o both sides equal −∞. For t=1 the expression is simply a_1≤U, omitting the zero-coefficient term. Together with U≼uα, this proves membership in the exact stretching class E_env(P^k,κ,uα), without invoking envelope equality.

For uniqueness within the stated radial family, another smooth-off-pole solution V has nonnegative nondecreasing flux aV=r(b+V)' by the k≥2 Hessian test. Its equation implies (aV^k)'=Fq', hence aV^k=Fq+C. Zero central flux forces C=0. Thus aV=Aq, V'=U', and V−U is constant. Hyperplane normalization fixes the constant. No nonsymmetric uniqueness is asserted.

Finally write r=|ξ|², ρ=|ξ|, ξ∈R^(2k). Off zero,
∇R=2R'ξ, D²R=2R'I+4R''ξ⊗ξ.
By (4), |∇R|≤Cρ^(2δ−1)(1−2logρ)^(α−2). For δ≥1/2 this tends to zero, including equality because α−2<0. Also |R−R0|/ρ→0. The residual is differentiable at zero with zero derivative and has continuous gradient: it is C1. For δ≥1, its Hessian tends to zero and |∇R|/ρ≤Cr^(δ−1)L^(α−2)→0. The gradient is differentiable at zero with derivative zero, and the Hessian is continuous: it is C2, including δ=1.

For δ≥1/2, the bounded gradient gives local Lipschitz regularity. For δ<1/2 put λ=2δ<1. Dropping the bounded logarithmic factor gives |R−R0|≤Cρ^λ and |∇R|≤Cρ^(λ−1). Given ξ,ζ, set d=|ξ−ζ| and Mρ=max(|ξ|,|ζ|). If d≥Mρ/2, the first bound gives a Cd^λ difference. Otherwise the segment stays at radius at least Mρ/2, and the gradient bound gives Cd Mρ^(λ−1)≤Cd^λ. This proves Hölder exponent min(1,2δ). Only the residual crosses the pole; U(o) remains −∞.

notes.summary: D is proved: Euler-flat relative density error implies a smoothly flat actual residual at the canonical pole.
notes.detailedSummary: Every Euler derivative of the cumulative error, its division by aα^k, and the flux difference is flat. Integrating the flux difference makes every ordinary radial derivative of R−R0 flat. Composition with |z|² gives a smooth residual whose derivatives all vanish at o. This requires the stated relative-density hypothesis, not determinant decay alone.
notes.text:
Under B put E=r d/dr and assume E^j g=O(r^N) for every N,j≥0. Here flatness means bounds of every power, with constants permitted to depend on the derivative and power.

In the notation of n2–n3, ET=−1/(1+r), and higher Euler derivatives of T are bounded near zero. Product and chain rules in the explicit flux formula give E^j aα=O(L^(α−1)) and E^j S=O(L^(−β)) for each j, with S=aα^k and β=k(1−α). Euler derivatives of inverse powers of aα and S grow at most as powers of L. Such factors preserve flatness because rL^M→0 for every fixed M.

The cumulative error H=∫_0^r g dS is flat: applying |g(t)|≤C_M t^M for any M>0 and the S' bound gives |H|≤C_M r^M L^(−β−1). For higher derivatives, EH=g ES, and E^jH is a sum of products of Euler derivatives of g and S. Hence every E^jH is flat. Division by S makes ε=H/S Euler-flat. Repeated chain rules for the smooth function (1+ε)^(1/k)−1, followed by multiplication by aα, show that Δ=Aq−aα is Euler-flat.

For h=R−R0, n3 gives h=∫_0^r Δ(t)dt/t and Eh=Δ. Integrating |Δ|≤C_Mr^M shows h is flat, and the Euler identity gives all higher Euler derivatives flat. The exact identity (d/dr)^j=r^(−j)E(E−1)…(E−j+1) converts these into flat ordinary derivatives by choosing a larger power first.

Define h(0)=0. Its derivatives extend by zero at zero; flat difference quotients prove differentiability of each extension. Induction gives a smooth one-variable function flat at zero, extendable by zero to negative arguments. Therefore h(|z|²) is smooth with every derivative zero at o. This proves D for the actual residual. U retains its canonical −∞ value. Density smoothness only off o, or determinant vanishing alone, does not supply this hypothesis.

notes.summary: E is proved with explicit compact cutoffs, exact probability normalization, the stated leading constants, sharp subcritical thresholds, and a nonzero smoothly flat perturbation.
notes.detailedSummary: Balanced cutoffs give positive q_c=qα[1+c(r^δχ0−B0χ1)] for small c. Elementary integral asymptotics yield Δ~cα(1−α)r^δL^(α−2)/δ and R−R0~cα(1−α)r^δL^(α−2)/δ². The real gradient and tangential Hessian eigenvalue prove all requested failures below the thresholds. Replacing r^δ by exp(−1/r) gives an actual nonzero flat example.
notes.text:
For explicit cutoffs define σ(t)=0 for t≤0, σ(t)=1 for t≥1, and for 0<t<1 set
σ(t)=e^(−1/t)/[e^(−1/t)+e^(−1/(1−t))].
Define βb(t)=exp(4−1/[t(1−t)]) for 0<t<1 and zero otherwise. Differentiation of the exponentially flat endpoint factors proves smoothness; βb is nonnegative with maximum one. For small ε>0 put χ0(r)=1−σ((r−ε)/ε) and χ1(r)=βb((r−4ε)/ε). Thus χ0=1 for r≤ε and vanishes for r≥2ε, while χ1 is supported in the disjoint annulus 4ε≤r≤5ε. These radial cutoffs are smooth on the compact projective space: χ0 is constant near o and both vanish near infinity.

With dμ=d(aα^k)=qακ^k in radial integration, set Iδ=∫r^δχ0dμ, J1=∫χ1dμ, and B0=Iδ/J1. Both integrals are finite and positive. If 0<c<1/[2B0||χ1||∞], then 1+c(r^δχ0−B0χ1)>1/2. Therefore q_c=qα[1+c(r^δχ0−B0χ1)] is positive off o, smooth there and at infinity, and has exact integral 1+c(Iδ−B0J1)=1. It is comparable to qα near the pole, so is L1 and belongs to no Lp, p>1. It satisfies B, with g=c r^δ near zero. A density value at the measure-zero pole can be assigned arbitrarily; potential pole values remain canonical.

For its actual B solution, H_c=F_{q_c}−S satisfies on 0<r<ε
H_c=c∫_0^r t^δS'(t)dt,
S'(t)~kα^k(1−α)t^(−1)L(t)^(−β−1).
For γ<0, the elementary equivalence
∫_0^r t^(δ−1)L(t)^γdt~r^δL(r)^γ/δ
follows by setting t=r e^(−v): after division by r^δL(r)^γ, the integral becomes ∫_0^∞e^(−δv)(1+v/L(r))^γdv, dominated by e^(−δv), and tends to 1/δ. Hence
H_c~[ckα^k(1−α)/δ]r^δL^(−β−1).
Taylor expansion of the kth root, using H_c/S→0, gives
Δ_c=A_{q_c}−aα~[cα(1−α)/δ]r^δL^(α−2).
It follows that
R_c'~[cα(1−α)/δ]r^(δ−1)L^(α−2),
R_c(r)−R_c(0)~[cα(1−α)/δ²]r^δL^(α−2).
Here R_c(0) denotes the finite residual limit, not a finite value of U_c.

In real coordinates, |∇R_c|=2√r|R_c'|, which diverges for δ<1/2. Every direction perpendicular to ξ has Hessian eigenvalue 2R_c', which diverges for δ<1. Such directions exist in R^(2k). The decaying logarithmic factor cannot counteract either negative power of r. If 2δ<1, along a radial line the quotient |R_c(ξ)−R_c(0)|/|ξ|^γ is comparable to |ξ|^(2δ−γ)(1−2log|ξ|)^(α−2), and diverges for every γ>2δ. Thus no larger conventional Hölder exponent holds. Together with n3 this proves the stated thresholds cannot be lowered, while retaining both critical endpoint conclusions.

For the flat example replace r^δχ0 by e^(−1/r)χ0, with its zero value at r=0, and balance using Bflat=(∫e^(−1/r)χ0dμ)/J1. Small positive c gives the same positivity and probability conclusions. Near zero g=c e^(−1/r); every Euler derivative is this exponential times a polynomial in 1/r, hence O(r^N) for every N. B and D apply. The residual minus its finite limit is smoothly flat. The perturbation and residual are nonconstant: H_c>0 near zero, so Δ_c>0 and R_c'>0 there.

The light audit uses k=3, α=0.6, δ=0.25. Scaled flux ratios are 0.922382149707019625, 0.991319357839629744, and 0.999121212278095049 at −log r=100,1000,10000. For ε=0.01 it finds B0≈2.52948236806221854 and a safe c≈0.0708319163915406593. These are numerical observations, not exhaustive verification or proof. Exact normalization and asymptotics follow from the arguments above. Rerun: python verify_radial.py > verification_output.txt.

notes.summary: G is proved, including zeros at infinity and an explicit open zero annulus with a globally smooth residual constant near the pole.
notes.detailedSummary: Cumulative mass remains positive at every finite radius and equals one at infinity, so the root defining the flux is smooth through every off-pole density zero. Explicit disjoint removal/restoration cutoffs give q0=qα(1−ηa+Bηb), with exact mass one, equality to qα near the pole and infinity, and an open zero annulus. Its actual solution has the prescribed ordinary type and a globally smooth residual.
notes.text:
Under B, n3 proves Fq(r)>0 at every finite r>0. Smoothness of q makes Fq smooth; its kth root is smooth on the positive range. Consequently Aq and U cross every finite-radius density zero smoothly, including zeros of infinite order and whole zero annuli. This uses cumulative positivity, not Hessian invertibility. At infinity Fq=1, and the η formula in n3 proves smoothness even when the density vanishes on the hyperplane. Thus U and its residual are smooth across every off-pole density zero.

For explicit compact data use σ and βb from n5 and set
ηa(r)=σ(2(r−1))[1−σ(2(r−7/2))],
ηb(r)=βb(r−5).
The first cutoff lies between zero and one, is supported in [1,4], and equals one on [3/2,7/2]. The second is a nonzero nonnegative bump supported in [5,6]. They vanish near o and infinity and are smooth radial functions on the compact space. Put Ia=∫ηa dμ>0, Jb=∫ηb dμ>0, B=Ia/Jb, and
q0=qα[1−ηa+Bηb].
The multiplier is nonnegative, vanishes on the nonempty open annulus 3/2<r<7/2, and equals one for r<1 and r>6. Its integral is exactly 1−Ia+BJb=1. The density is smooth off o and at infinity. Equality to qα near the pole gives L1 and failure of every Lp, p>1. It satisfies B with zero error near zero, for every positive δ.

The actual canonical solution U0 supplied by n3 has sole pole o, is ordinarily equivalent to uα, and belongs to the exact stretching class. For r<1, its cumulative mass equals S and its flux equals aα. Therefore the actual residual U0−uα has derivative zero there. It extends constantly across o. Everywhere else, including transitions, the zero annulus, and infinity, both potentials are smooth. Hence its residual is globally smooth. On the zero annulus the flux is a positive constant, so the local radial potential has a zero radial Hessian eigenvalue but remains smooth. U0(o) still equals −∞.

For k=3, α=0.6, the audit reports Ia≈0.27347816544895543, B≈24.4405059274834508, and balanced total mass 1.0; cutoff checks at r=2 and r=0.001 pass. These observations supplement, but do not prove, the exact construction. Rerun: python verify_radial.py > verification_output.txt. No general principle based only on local density smoothness is asserted, and weighted extremals remain unanswered.

notes.summary: F is proved conditionally: zero factor lower mass forces a genuinely nonclosed positive product background with zero lower mass, while the explicit singular pullback has finite mass without BMP.
notes.detailedSummary: Bounded factor potentials approaching zero mass pull back with product masses multiplied by binom(m+k,m). Closedness would contradict the bounded Stokes identity. The actual singular pullback measure is obtained directly from bounded truncation locality and explicit integrability. Ordinary equivalence, stretching membership, and residual regularity pull back. Factor existence, BMP, and singular-type volume thresholds are not asserted.
notes.text:
Assume F's antecedent without asserting any example: (X0,h0) is a connected compact Hermitian m-fold with v−(h0)=inf_{b bounded h0-psh}∫(h0+dd^c b)^m=0. Put V0=∫h0^m>0, N=m+k, and H=π0^*h0+π1^*κ on X0×P^k. It is smooth positive, hence big with genuine potential zero, reference metric H, and ε=1.

If h0 were closed, n1's bounded Stokes identity would make every bounded potential's mass equal V0, contradicting v−=0. Thus dh0≠0. Pullback by the submersion π0 is injective on forms, so dH=π0^*dh0≠0. This establishes genuine nonclosedness.

Choose bounded canonical h0-psh b_j whose masses tend to zero, using the infimum definition. Their pullbacks are bounded H-psh. Bounded expansion and pullback compatibility from n1 give
(H+dd^cπ0^*b_j)^N=binom(N,m)π0^*(h0+dd^c b_j)^m∧π1^*κ^k.
